must_remember: Adiabatic demagnetization is used to achieve temperatures well below $1\text{ K}$, typically down to the millikelvin range.
The technique was first proposed by P. Debye (1926) and W. Giauque (1927).
Paramagnetic salts containing ions with unpaired electrons, such as gadolinium sulfate, are utilized as working substances.
The cooling cycle consists of two primary stages: Isothermal Magnetization and Adiabatic Demagnetization.
Total entropy of the salt is the sum of lattice entropy and magnetic entropy.
Absolute zero ($0\text{ K}$) cannot be reached in a finite number of steps in accordance with the Third Law of Thermodynamics.
Residual interactions between magnetic ions and external heat leaks prevent reaching absolute zero.
Curie's Law of Paramagnetism states that magnetization $M = \frac{C \cdot B}{T}$ under high temperatures and weak magnetic fields.

glossary.meaning: A thermodynamic technique used to produce extremely low temperatures by rapidly reducing the magnetic field surrounding an insulated paramagnetic salt.
The portion of a system's entropy associated with the orientation and disorder of magnetic dipoles or spins.
A material-specific constant that characterizes the magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic substance as a function of temperature.
A substance containing ions with unpaired electrons that exhibit temporary magnetization in the presence of an external magnetic field.
A peak in the specific heat capacity of a solid at low temperatures, arising from a finite number of discrete energy levels.

comparisons.title: Isothermal Magnetization vs Adiabatic Demagnetization
rows: In thermal contact with a constant temperature bath (e.g., liquid helium)
Magnetic field is rapidly reduced to zero
Magnetic entropy decreases as dipoles align
Magnetic entropy increases while lattice entropy drops; total entropy is constant
Heat of magnetization is rejected to the surroundings
No heat exchange with the surroundings ($dQ = 0$)
Temperature drops significantly due to energy transfer to spins
